vignette:
The Weight of the Diagnosis

Samuel is a 68-year-old widowed policy analyst who has spent the better part of four decades shaping health equity frameworks for governments across sub-Saharan Africa. He is a man accustomed to reading systems, anticipating failure points, and designing solutions before crises fully arrive. He is not, by his own admission, a man who has ever expected to become the crisis himself.

Three years ago, Samuel was diagnosed with stage three colorectal cancer. He describes the moment the oncologist spoke those words as a kind of rupture — not dramatic in the way he might have imagined, but quiet and absolute, like a door closing in a room he hadn't known he was standing in. He sat in the consultation chair, still wearing his reading glasses, and felt the floor beneath him become something unreliable. He had recently lost his wife, Amara, to a stroke eighteen months prior, and the diagnosis arrived into a life already hollowed by grief. He remembers thinking, with a clarity that still disturbs him, I am going to die alone in a foreign hospital.

The treatment that followed — surgery, chemotherapy, a prolonged hospital admission complicated by infection — was grueling in ways Samuel struggles to articulate. He describes lying in the ward at night, listening to monitors and the sounds of other patients, certain on several occasions that he would not survive until morning. There were moments of acute medical crisis during his recovery that required emergency intervention, and it is these nights, he says, that live most persistently inside him now.

Samuel completed treatment successfully. His oncologist uses the word remarkable. Samuel does not feel remarkable. He feels like a man who crossed a bridge that is no longer there.

He returned to his work in policy analysis, initially finding comfort in the familiar architecture of reports and consultations. But increasingly, the work itself has become a source of distress. He sits at his desk drafting briefs on healthcare infrastructure and finds his mind hijacked by the smell of antiseptic, the cold weight of an IV line, the particular fluorescent quality of hospital light at 3 a.m. He will be mid-sentence in a document about palliative care access and suddenly he is back in that ward, convinced he is dying. He has submitted two reports with significant errors in recent months, something that would have been unthinkable to him before.

Sleep has become a negotiation he rarely wins. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart pounding, certain that something is catastrophically wrong with his body. He checks his pulse. He sits at the edge of the bed in the dark apartment he once shared with Amara and waits for the fear to recede. Some nights it does not. He has attended three emergency departments in the past year for symptoms that, each time, proved to be panic.

Samuel avoids his own physician now, rescheduling appointments repeatedly. He knows, analytically, that surveillance is essential after cancer treatment. He knows this the way he knows policy — intellectually, structurally, without feeling. But the thought of entering a medical building, of sitting in a waiting room, of hearing a doctor's careful, measured tone, fills him with a dread so physical it bends him forward. He has not had his six-month follow-up scan.

He tells himself he is being rational. That after everything, a man deserves peace. But in quieter moments, he acknowledges something closer to the truth — that he is afraid of what they might find, and equally, inexplicably afraid of the relief of finding nothing. As though his vigilance is the only thing keeping him alive.

Samuel comes to sessions dressed carefully, speaks precisely, and often begins by asking whether what he is experiencing is normal for someone who has been through what he has been through. He is a man who has spent his life building systems to protect others from preventable harm, sitting now in the unfamiliar position of being someone who cannot protect himself.
